sections.h2: Who sets and collects property tax in Massachusetts?
sections.html:
Each of the state's 351 cities and towns assesses and collects its own property tax, so the bill for a house depends on the municipality, not the county. The Division of Local Services, part of the Department of Revenue, oversees the system, and your local board of assessors holds the property record card for your house.

Value is set as of January 1 for the fiscal year that follows. The Appellate Tax Board's guide gives an example: fiscal year 2025 runs July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025, and its valuation date is January 1, 2024. For a seller, that gap explains why a bill can reflect a value set well before you list the house.

sections.h2: What is Proposition 2½ and how does it limit your tax bill?
sections.html:
Proposition 2½ limits what a city or town can raise in total, not what any single owner pays. The Division of Local Services describes two restrictions: the levy cannot exceed 2.5% of the community's total assessed value, and the yearly increase is capped at 2.5% of the prior year's levy limit plus new growth.

Voters can raise the amount above that only through an override, a debt exclusion or a capital exclusion. The same article reports that statewide excess levy capacity was $918 million in fiscal 2025, equal to 3.9% of the levy limit, and that more than half of the municipalities (186) had excess capacity below 1% of the maximum levy.

Individual bills still move, because the total levy is divided among all taxable property. When your neighbors' values rise faster than yours, your share can fall even when your own value goes up.

sections.h2: When are Massachusetts property tax bills due?
sections.html:
Due dates depend on how your municipality bills. In quarterly towns, installments are generally due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. In towns that bill twice a year, a bill is generally due 30 days after it is mailed.

Billing styleGeneral due dates
QuarterlyAugust 1, November 1, February 1, May 1
Twice a yearThirty days from the mailing of the bill

The face of your actual tax bill states the due date for payment and for abatement requests. If a bank or mortgage company pays your tax, the Appellate Tax Board's guide stresses that it is still your responsibility to make sure the payment arrives on time.

sections.h2: How do you apply for an abatement?
sections.html:
You file an abatement application with your local board of assessors on the approved form, on or before the due date of the first installment of the actual tax bill. In quarterly municipalities that date is generally February 1, and in twice-a-year municipalities it is generally 30 days after the bill is mailed.

  • Forms are available from the local assessors' office.
  • An abatement is a reduction in tax, usually granted when you can show fair cash value is lower than the assessed value. It can also be granted for an exemption or an improper classification.
  • Fair cash value is the price a willing seller and a willing buyer would agree on in an arm's-length sale, with neither under compulsion.
  • The postmark rule treats the postmark date as the filing date for mail sent through the U.S. Postal Service or an approved delivery service.

Assessors have three months to act. They can deny, grant in full or in part, or do nothing, and they must send written notice within ten days of acting. If they do nothing, the application is deemed denied after three calendar months, not 90 days.

sections.h2: How do you appeal to the Appellate Tax Board?
sections.html:
You file with the Appellate Tax Board within three months of the assessors' action, or within three months of the deemed denial if they never acted. When the notice shows two dates, count from the date of action, not the mailing date.

Three requirements are jurisdictional, meaning the board cannot hear the case without them: timely payment of the tax, a timely abatement application on the approved form, and a timely appeal. The guide says no exceptions can be made. There is one narrow relief on payment: the board can still hear an appeal if the tax due for the year is $5,000 or less, or if you paid at least the average tax of one of the three prior years.

  • The filing fee depends on assessed value under the board's Schedule of Entry Fees.
  • Most single-family appeals use the informal procedure, which waives most further appeal rights.
  • It usually takes four months to a year to get a hearing, most single-family hearings last one to two hours, and a decision arrives within roughly three months.

sections.h2: What must you prove at the hearing?
sections.html:
You carry the burden. A tax assessment is presumed valid, so you must show that the fair cash value of your house is below the assessed value, as of the January 1 valuation date. Saying that the tax went up 20% generally does not succeed, according to the board's guide.

The guide recommends describing the house in detail, reviewing the assessors' record card, and gathering sales of comparable properties that match on type, location, size, timing and condition, with adjustments for differences. You may also use comparable assessments or hire an expert appraiser. Documents must reach the board and the other side at least seven days before the hearing.

There is one exception to the presumption. If the board set a value for one year and assessors raise it in either of the next two fiscal years, the burden shifts to the assessors to justify the increase.

sections.h2: What happens if property tax goes unpaid?
sections.html:
Unpaid property tax or water and sewer charges become a lien, and the city or town can eventually take the house. The Land Court describes the steps: after 30 days unpaid, the municipality can send a demand, and if you do not pay within 14 days, it can record a tax taking at the Registry of Deeds.

  • Six or twelve months later, the holder of the tax title can file a foreclosure complaint in the Land Court.
  • A private party can become the tax title owner, for example by buying bundled tax bills or winning an auction.
  • You can file an answer and ask for a hearing, where you may offer to redeem by paying everything owed or ask for a payment plan.
  • If you do not pay by the date the court sets, the court may enter a judgment of foreclosure, which ends your right to get the property back.

A foreclosed owner may try to recover money if the house was worth more than the debt. That is a reason to deal with a tax taking early, before it reaches the Land Court.

sections.h2: How does tax due affect selling a house in Massachusetts?
sections.html:
A recorded tax taking is a title problem that must be cleared before a clean sale, and paying everything owed ends the city or town's claim before a final foreclosure judgment. Ask the closing attorney how any unpaid tax will be handled at the table.

Before listing, request a payoff figure from the collector's office, check your assessors' record for errors, and note any abatement deadline you may miss by selling. The guide does not cover how a pending abatement transfers at a sale, so ask the assessors' office and your closing attorney.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to file a Massachusetts property tax abatement?
faqs.a: It is the due date of the first installment of the actual tax bill. That is generally February 1 in quarterly-billing towns and about 30 days after mailing in twice-a-year towns. Check the face of your bill.

faqs.q: How long do assessors have to decide an abatement?
faqs.a: Three months. If they do not act, the application is deemed denied after three calendar months, and you then have three months to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay the tax while I appeal?
faqs.a: Generally yes. The Appellate Tax Board needs the tax paid on time to have jurisdiction, with limited exceptions when the tax is $5,000 or less or you paid the average of a prior year.
It limits the total levy a municipality can raise. The levy cannot exceed 2.5% of total assessed value, and it can rise by 2.5% of the prior levy limit plus new growth unless voters approve more.

faqs.q: Can the city take my house for unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. After a demand and 14 days, the city or town can record a tax taking, and a Land Court foreclosure can follow. You can redeem by paying all taxes, interest and fees before a final judgment.
